findings.evidence: The resolution is capacity/scheduling — additional hosts, chunked prefill, admission control/backpressure, or P/D disaggregation. ... Hosts were raised from H=1 to H=21. That is the capacity floor, which is the max of the named screens, not the prefill compute screen alone: case (i)’s prefill screen needs ⌈18.6⌉ = 19 hosts, but the KV-residency / Little’s-Law screen needs ⌈344/17⌉ = 21 hosts at the peak and therefore binds (Ch 8 §3; Ch 17).
findings.issue: The mini-case resolution says the host count was raised to H = 21, but the chapter has not established that the described deployment actually has the 17 KV slots per host used by the Little’s-Law screen. The chapter’s own running case starts from a single host and diagnoses a prefill oversubscription; jumping to H = 21 by importing the canonical 17-slot screen is a cross-scenario substitution. The text presents H = 21 as the resolution of this mini-case, but the canonical 17-slot figure belongs to the 9.5K-token resident-basis geometry, not necessarily to the mini-case’s named deployment. This is a scope/referent ambiguity: the reader cannot tell whether 21 hosts is the answer for the mini-case or merely the canonical workload’s separate screen.
findings.fix_instruction: State explicitly that the mini-case adopts the canonical 9.5K-token resident-basis host geometry and the same 17-slot KV screen; otherwise recompute the KV slot count for the mini-case’s actual resident token count and context distribution before quoting H = 21. Add one sentence separating the mini-case’s measured/inferred host count from the canonical Ch 17 screen.

findings.evidence: The p99 position is 1 + (N−1) × 0.99 = 9,900.01. The sorted-sample ranks are 9,900 → 1.30 s and 9,901 → 5.0 s, so 1.30 + 0.01 × (5.0 − 1.30) ≈ 1.33 s: the interpolation lands just past the largest non-straggler draw, between it and the first straggler.
findings.issue: The interpolation explanation says the p99 position is 9,900.01, but the sorted-sample ranks used are 9,900 and 9,901. With the standard percentile interpolation formula, the fractional part of the 1-based rank should be applied between rank 9,900 and rank 9,901, so the interpolation fraction is 0.01, not 0.01 of the difference between those ranks? Actually the arithmetic is correct: 1.30 + 0.01 × (5.0 − 1.30) = 1.337. The wording “lands just past the largest non-straggler draw” is the real issue: it implies the largest non-straggler is at rank 9,900, but the interpolation is between the 9,900th and 9,901st sorted values; the text does not state what the 9,900th value is or whether it is the largest non-straggler. This is a minor clarity issue, not an arithmetic error.
findings.fix_instruction: State the sorted values explicitly: “rank 9,900 = 1.30 s, rank 9,901 = 5.0 s; the interpolated p99 is 1.30 + 0.01 × (5.0 − 1.30) = 1.337 s.” Avoid the phrase “largest non-straggler draw” unless the rank-9,900 value is identified as such.

findings.evidence: Figure 6.2's inline plot label reads "SLO 2 s (TTFT budget)", while the same figure's caption states the 2 s line is "the p95 TTFT ceiling (Ch 4, Table 4-1 Latency row; Canonical Workload box), not the 1.2 s design budget". Ch. 4 §4.3 fixes the terminology: "The two thresholds are not interchangeable: 1.2 s is the design budget, ≤ 2 s is the p95 ceiling the budget relaxes to"; Ch. 6 §6.3.1 likewise: "the 2 s p95 TTFT ceiling (the SLO itself is stated at p95, Ch 4) — a ceiling above the 1.2 s design budget, not a second budget".
findings.issue: The figure's internal label calls the 2 s line the "TTFT budget", conflating the 1.2 s design budget with the 2 s p95 ceiling — precisely the conflation the book repeatedly forbids — and contradicting the figure's own caption on the same page.
findings.fix_instruction: Relabel the 2 s line in Fig. 6.2 to "p95 TTFT SLO 2 s (ceiling)" (or "SLO 2 s — p95 TTFT ceiling"), reserving the word "budget" for the 1.2 s figure; verify no other figure reuses "TTFT budget" for the 2 s line.
